Dear Ms. Crouse,

One needn’t have read Montagu’s The Natural Superiority of Women to know the typical woman gets more done in one day without complaint than the typical man does in a week.

And now that the playing field is more level, their tenacity and adaptability is simply becoming more abundantly clear.

But a very wise woman of renowned high IQ was once asked what a person could do to maximize his or her own intelligence, and she responded this way:

Find the two largest trash cans you can, and actual one and an imaginary, and throw out absolutely everything you do not need from your physical surroundings and then do the same with the refuse in your mind.

Subtraction. Relentless “giving up” of the foolishness inside and out so you may have laser focus on the things that matter.

Our entire present day is laser-focused on precisely the opposite proposition. So I concur with your suggestion. And on a personal note, I took high-IQ lady up on her advice fifty years ago, and reading all of Shakespeare last year was just one of the many fruits of the sagacity of “giving up” silly things (such as TV) so you might gain better ones.

Cordially

comments.name: Jack McIntyre

I live in the shadow of Lone Peak in the Wasatch Mountains of Utah. I have been with these mountains for more than 50 years. 

When I arrived here we had year-round snow in high crags above 10,000 feet. We had a big glacier on Lone Peak.

It’s gone. 

We had a glacier on Mt. Timpanogos to my south. Gone. There was a substantial glacier on Mt. Nebo that we would climb and ski in the middle of summer. 

Gone. 

The Wasatch run 165 miles north to south from the Idaho border to central Utah. Many of it’s high peaks were snowcapped all year. They are all bare rock now. There have been many slides as the underlying frozen water melted and rocks sheared off. 

We baked away near or above 100 degrees F for three months this summer and had fires all over the place - again. We are running out of water. 

But the Trump crowd says “climate change is a hoax.” 

As he grabs the oil in Venezuela. Oh well. This trend can’t be reversed without a major global die off of humans.

There were only aisles in his house because it was so packed. This past April his house burned to the ground. Nothing was insured. He only survived because an emergency room nurse down the street ran to the burning house and pulled him off the back porch where he had collapsed. Hoarding is dangerous. comments.name: Emotional Cheese

The LW answered their own question several times—the husband does not want help. Period. 
It seems like, at this point, all the LW and other concerned family/friends can do is check in on him (by phone, text, etc.) to make sure he’s alive and unharmed. That’s it. 
My experience with a family member and also  an ex who were hoarders taught me the power of this disease (and it is a disease). Hoarders don’t want help. 
Sometimes they are ashamed of their situation (as was my ex). Other times they really believe that they need everything they keep (as in my family member).  
Regardless, it’s a folly to think that you can help them. If they ever decide to do something about all their stuff, it has to come from them (and, tragically, it may be the result of a dire emergency).

comments.name: Jordan
comments.body: Regarding the threads emerging about global warming and greenhouse gas emissions, we tend to self flagellate in the US. I’m a card carrying Democrat, but the truth is this is a global challenge, and a nuanced one at that. Wealthy countries like Singapore, Switzerland, Luxembourg, Ireland, Norway, and many others (especially Europeans) are responsible for importing more greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions per capita than Americans. America just has a much larger industrial manufacturing sector, and we do consume more total because of our geography and history - newer countries spread across vast land/area including the US, Canada, and Australia have higher combined GHG per capita largely because we drive more (by necessity). Large land mass, newer housing and roads, spread out further than the centuries old cities and villages and cities in Europe. We also build living spaces to heat, cool, and run. So they may suffer through their non AC using summers, but behind the scenes the wealthy Europeans still contribute to the problem. At the end of the day, this is why the “useless” UN exists - global challenges require global coordination. Alas we are too caught up with pointing fingers and also perhaps a hint of lying to ourselves about our ideals vs. needs / reality.

"Stand up, real big and tall. Shoulders back, chin up. Put a tough swagger in your step and a smirk on your face. Anybody who sees you will think you’re the one who’s going to cause trouble.”

I've followed this wonderful advice all my life. Now, as a petite woman grazing 5' tall, I wouldn't walk anywhere by myself late at night. That said, the ability to project toughness is a useful trait in other settings.

I was trying cases inside courtrooms right after I turned 24 years old. Jurors were often amused at me. I understood that I needed some way to project myself other than "cute little thing". 

This didn't mean projecting anger, hostility. I knew that as a young woman, those qualities would work against me. 

So instead I made it a point to watch the successful litigators. They oozed confidence. They were at ease with themselves. They were comfortable speaking up in public. Then I just started emulating them. 

One more quality - I soon learned that even if I didn't feel that confidence, even if I didn't have all that experience - especially in the first few years - I could fake it really well. And this is when I learned that this is what most of my male colleagues (in those years, they were all men) were doing anyway!

And I knew I succeeded when my daughter, then about 10 years old, told me, "Mom, if you were tall, you'd be really scary!"

Best to everyone here on the MD stoop this morning,
OC

Time to be honest.  

My last name is Campbell.  

And so, never having visited Scotland in my life--

--I'd love to go there.  

But I don't think I'd require so much luxury.  

I've talked to a young woman who (with her daughter) spent some months in Edinburgh. 

She could not say enough good about the place.  The two of them (I gather) had a glorious time.  

She told me that the natives of Edinburgh and the Americans coasting in for a visit--

--dress rather differently.  

The native Scots are partial to quieter colors.  And not quite so much clothing.  Guess they're used to whatever frigid winds come barreling in.  

The Americans wear lots more clothing.  And are partial to--

--how to say this?  Colors that attract the eye.  Colorful stuff.  

If I ever go there,  I'll remember to eschew the bolder colors.  

But fewer clothes?  I'm sorry, my hardy Scottish forebears!

He too was about seventy seven when he--

comments.name: Ithaca Reader

When historian and strategist Carter Malkasian wrote that the U.S. military "fights to win," he was pointing to a fundamental paradox in modern military culture. On paper, most militaries exist to secure national objectives. Yet, when a war begins to turn sour or is unwinnable, institutional momentum rarely shifts toward a graceful exit; instead, it doubles down on the fight.

Our military is trained, structured, and socialized around the concept of victory. To accept defeat or a stalemate is to contradict the core purpose of the profession. Soldiers, officers, and especially generals view quitting not as a rational pivot, but as a failure.

Admitting failure carries a devastating career cost for military leadership and political figures alike. Generals who advocate for withdrawal risk being labeled as defeatists or insubordinate, while politicians fear being blamed for losing. Staying the course is frequently perceived as the only safe choice.

Once lives have been lost and immense treasure spent, admitting defeat becomes morally agonizing. Stopping the war forces leaders and society to confront the grim reality that those past sacrifices were in vain. Continuing to fight offers a way to keep the meaning of those sacrifices alive, creating a powerful barrier to withdrawal.

Ultimately, a military fights even when losing because stopping requires an admission of failure that institutional structures are simply not designed to accept.

comments.body: In Greensboro, NC we have some ever-present reminders of Maria Edgeworth.  Edgeworth Street is downtown adjacent to the property featuring Blandwood, the mansion of progressive Governor John Motley Morehead (1796-1866).  Morehead had five daughters to educate, and he did so by founding Edgeworth Female Seminary in 1840.  He named the school for the author whose work he greatly admired and to be a significant influence.  Edgeworth and Morehead were convinced that women should have equal intellectual educations, and Morehead brought that conviction into being.  I believe that the school was successful for twenty or more years, but was closed during the Civil War and the building was lost. comments.name: KJB

Edgeworth has indeed been well known and her works have been taught and studied for centuries. She was so popular that her pedagogical works and children's literature sparked a series of schools devoted to her teachings. These schools were not just in Ireland but they were also in the United States--there is a twin in western Pennsylvania that has one, for example. 

She was a great proponent of teaching girls and boys literature, history, languages, and particularly sciences, this in addition to her literary works. I'm thinking of Belinda in which she introduces a character with breast cancer, The Absentee in which she discusses the devastating effects of absentee English colonization on the Irish people and economy, Castle Rackent where she introduces the economic disparities between the generations of landholders and the native Irish as well as the last generation's craven antisemitism. Her Essay on Irish Bulls is an important work on the linguistic and rhetorical differences between English and Irish.

She did not make distinctions between the education of girls and boys. She has been very important in the fields of educational history, Irish history, literature, linguistics, and Jewish studies. Several years ago there was a n exhibit of her books at the Toronto library.

To call her forgotten or erased is simply untrue.

This was an interesting anecdote about bank incompetence, but it didn’t really illuminate the core problem.

These scams are not intended to remove you from your house; the goal is to extract money via fraudulent purchase or lease, taking advantage of detection lag.

The root cause of this problem, and the reason that everyone in this country feels like there are scams everywhere, is that white collar crime is at the lowest prosecution point in the modern era at a time when it should be the highest. 

Since I deal with this stuff for a living, I can say with confidence the local police and prosecutors are terrible at it. Furthermore, the current administration has gutted white-collar enforcement in favor of other priorities. Some of those priorities include taking experienced FBI financial crime SA’s and SSA‘s and allocating them to immigrant roundup task forces. 

Nobody voted for me so I don’t get to decide. But I would prefer law-enforcement to focus on white-collar crime.

comments.body:
Dolly Parton's passing has all of America ruminating on so many things, but perhaps none more than that she was goodness personified. 

- She earned her impressive living in a fashion that contributed to the arts/entertainment landscape, and harmed no one. 
- She used her well-gotten gains to fund endeavors (literacy, vaccine research, providing band uniforms to underfunded schools) that improved the lives of others, often on a national or global level, but often locally (and anonymously).
- She never turned her back on where she came from.
She did her family, herself, and her church proud.

The demise of small churches that helped produced the likes of her is regrettable in and of itself, but doubly so as these intimate, community gathering places are replaced by megachurches which -- let's be honest -- are essentially tax-free businesses, often wielding outsize political clout.

I hope church-goers (and also regular attendees of synagogues and mosques) can distinguish between the establishments that promote actual goodness (in words and action) and acceptance towards all of humanity, and those that inculcate a sense of superiority and judgment among their members. Only one is worth a contribution into the collection plate.

I grew up in a close knit anglophone community, part of a larger town with a francophone majority, north of Montreal , Quebec .
During the 1950’s , our beautiful little St Michael’s  Anglican Church was the the centerpiece .. Sunday  and holiday services , Sunday School , choir practice , baptisms, confirmations , weddings , summer socials , second hand clothing sales , and maybe most important of all inter- generational mixing and mutual support .
I moved away 50 years ago .. the Anglophone Anglican  community has mostly vanished , the Church is a sort of historical monument and privately owned for non religious purposes .
 I am not religious but when it came time after my mother’s death we organized an Anglican burial service in the volunteer maintained Anglican cemetery . 
So far away from the American South .. but I get it .

Doing so feels like thinking about the subject from a fantasy novel - it’s so unimaginable. And yet, by all accounts and honest understandings, this is the way Christianity is supposed to be. 

That Dolly Parton, the extraordinarily gifted and celebrated musician, business woman, actor, songwriter, singer, advocate, is being remembered and loved because of person she was … and the Christian life she lived … well beyond all her “accomplishments,” is an astounding testament to the power of the life she lived, and how she intentionally made every effort to remain kind, strong, grateful, effective and nonjudgmental.

Fascism is at its root an aesthetic movement; yes that aesthetic is derivative, constructed, tedious and violent (see e.g. Futurism), but the point is not only to control people, but to control their perception of reality. It is a game of conspiracies within conspiracies, in which the entire point is to be the one who is most inside the wall. This is why at its heart, all fascist governments have been essentially kleptocracies full of seething, warring interests. It is interesting that we are instead given the image of fascism as .. evil, sure, but also exceptionally efficient and inventive.

Why do I bring this up here? Because fascism obtains its power through the machinery of aesthetic manipulation. It knows that words and actions have real power; yes, to distort reality, to make people believe what you want them to believe.

Now, look at the word magic and the ideology behind Silicon Valley and finance capital in general. It’s a spectacle, full of public and private ritual. The price of entry is to swallow whatever drink you’re given. The ring was kept in a safe box whose key's location I knew. I was frightened that someone would notice it being missing, but my Mom had passed away and my Dad apparently had more important things on his mind.
